title: What You'll Build - A Website to Mint, Buy and Sell NFTs
section: 42. Minting NFTs and Building an NFT Marketplace like OpenSea
summary: Project overview for OpenD, an OpenSea-style NFT marketplace on the Internet Computer. Explains what fungibility means, how real NFTs reference off-chain storage, and the features the finished app will have.

concepts.heading: Fungible vs non-fungible
points: Fungible assets are interchangeable: any banknote of a given value can be swapped for another with no loss. The coins/tokens built earlier (Bitcoin, Ethereum, the course's DANG token) behave this way.
A non-fungible token (NFT) has a unique identifier and unique data, so no two are equivalent, like an original painting versus a perfect copy.
NFTs most often represent digital images; ownership is recorded on a blockchain.

concepts.heading: Marketplace context
points: OpenSea is the model: users list NFTs and others buy them, prices quoted in a crypto currency (ETH there), and the platform keeps a small percentage fee per sale (about 2.5%).
Takeaway for developers: running the marketplace platform can be more lucrative than being one creator.
Large mainstream sales (an auction-house sale of a digital art collection for tens of millions of dollars) show demand.

concepts.heading: Where NFT data usually lives
points: On most chains the token is a smart contract that stores a token URI pointing to the image, commonly on IPFS or even a company server. The image itself is not on-chain.

The demo follows an OpenSea item: its contract address leads to Etherscan, the contract exposes a token URI function, and passing the token id returns an IPFS identifier that resolves to a publicly accessible image URL.
In OpenD the image bytes are stored on-chain inside the Internet Computer canister, so the asset does not depend on an outside host.

concepts.heading: What OpenD will do
points: Inspired by CryptoPunks pixel-art characters. The course supplies six pixel-art images (drawn by the instructor, downloadable from the lecture resources) so no purchase is needed.
Minting: the user uploads an image and a name; this programmatically creates a new canister holding the NFT data (name, owner, image bytes).
My collection page: shows NFTs the logged-in user owns; each has a Sell button that asks for a price in DANG (the token from the previous project).
Discover page: lists all NFTs put up for sale; a user cannot buy their own listing but can buy others', paying in DANG, after which the NFT appears in their collection.
Simplified feature set compared with OpenSea, focusing on core ideas: programmatic canister creation, ownership transfer, and payment using a third-party token.
Stack: React frontend, Motoko backend on the Internet Computer.
(Extra) Skills practised: Motoko classes as canisters, actor classes, HashMaps and lists, React Router, authenticated calls from the previous lesson.

pitfalls: (Extra) Do not assume an NFT's image is on-chain elsewhere: URI-based NFTs can break if the host disappears; that is the weakness OpenD avoids.

gaps_and_ideas: Proposed lesson 'Fungible vs non-fungible': blurb comparing a token balance map to a unique-id ownership map.
Tasks: 1) classify examples as fungible or not; 2) sketch the data of one NFT (id, name, owner, image); 3) list the pages of OpenD and what each shows; 4) decide where each piece of data would live.
Starter code: a JS object mapping ids to owners for tokens vs NFTs.
Interactive demo idea: swap two coins (identical) versus two NFT cards (the swap changes ownership but not identity), with an on-chain vs URL storage toggle.
